title: The stolen blessing (Genesis 27)
hook: Jacob in goatskins deceives his blind father, and Esau weeps

segments.voice: Yesterday, the birthright: Esau's future, traded for red stew. Your line was not for a bowl of stew. Today, the same brothers, years later.

If you were inventing a holy book to make your people look good, you would not write this chapter. The man the whole nation will be named after, the grandson of Abraham, puts on his brother's clothes, ties goatskins to his arms so he'll feel hairy, carries in a dish his mother cooked, and lies to his blind, aging father's face, more than once. And it works. Genesis tells it in slow, painful detail, as if it wants you to sit in the room. Isaac is old, his eyes have failed, and he wants to bless his favorite son before he dies.
screen: `NOT HOW YOU'D WRITE YOUR HEROES.` → `GOATSKINS AND A BROTHER'S CLOTHES.` → `A BLIND FATHER, AND A LIE.`

segments.voice: First, the plan. Isaac sends Esau out to hunt game and make the savory meat he loves, so he can bless him. Rebecca overhears. She has Jacob bring two young goats, cooks them the way Isaac likes, dresses Jacob in Esau's best clothes, and covers his hands and neck with the skins. Jacob worries about being caught, and she says, upon me be thy curse, my son. Second, the scene. Isaac is suspicious. You came back so fast? Come close, let me feel you. Then the famous line, in the Douay-Rheims: "The voice indeed is the voice of Jacob; but the hands are the hands of Esau." He asks straight out, are you my son Esau? And Jacob says, I am. Isaac smells the field on his clothes, and blesses him with dew of heaven and fatness of the earth. Third, the other door. Jacob has barely left when Esau comes in with his dish. Who are you? Your firstborn, Esau. And Isaac trembles. Esau roars out with a great cry: "Bless me also, my father." Have you only one blessing, father? And he weeps, a grown man, a hunter. Fourth, what the Bible does with it. It doesn't hide it. Augustine read the trick as a mystery pointing beyond itself. Other readers simply let it stand: God's promise goes on through a family that lies, plays favorites and breaks. Esau says in his heart he'll kill his brother. Rebecca sends Jacob away for a few days, she says. Genesis never records her seeing him again.
screen: `A MOTHER'S PLAN, TWO YOUNG GOATS.` · `THE VOICE OF JACOB, THE HANDS OF ESAU.` · `ESAU'S GREAT CRY.` · `THE PROMISE GOES THROUGH A BROKEN HOME.` · then, large: `BLESS ME ALSO, MY FATHER.`

segments.voice: Let your memory go back, gently, to a time you let someone believe something that wasn't true: a version of events that made you look better, a credit you didn't correct. Don't punish yourself; just look at it the way Genesis does, plainly, and ask what one honest step would look like now. If you pray, bring it to God first.
Berakhah, blessing, in Hebrew: what Jacob stole from his blind father in his brother's clothes, while Esau wept too late. Today's word.
Your line: the bible doesn't hide it. Its heroes come with their flaws showing. That's day three hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Catholics examine their consciences before confession, and the Church teaches that lying offends against truth and that repairing harm done by a lie is part of making amends.

original.note: Hebrew: blessing. yesterday Jacob took the bekhorah, the birthright; today the berakhah.

trapdoor: what you thought: the hero tricks his way to the top.
what it means: the Bible tells, in slow detail, how its own family lied and broke, and how God's promise went on anyway.
what a scholar hears: bekhorah and berakhah, birthright and blessing, a pair of sound-alike words; Augustine read the trick as a mystery, other readers let it stand.

chat.says: Why would the Bible tell such an ugly story about Jacob, one of its heroes?
options: It doesn't hide it: God's promise goes on through a family that lies and breaks.
Because in the end Jacob confesses, and Esau gets the very same blessing.
Because the trick was Jacob's idea alone, to show how bad he really was.
chat.meaning: Genesis tells the deception in slow, plain detail. The promise goes on through a family that lies, plays favorites and breaks.

Augustine.meaning: an early Church teacher who read the trick as a mystery

Esau.meaning: Jacob's twin brother, the firstborn and a hunter

Douay-Rheims.meaning: the old Catholic English translation of the Bible

sources.quoted: The voice indeed is the voice of Jacob; but the hands are the hands of Esau.

notes: Douay-Rheims Genesis 27:22 and 27:34 quoted from memory; confirm.
27:38 ('Hast thou only one blessing, father?') paraphrased in modern words without quotation marks. 'Upon me be thy curse' (27:13) paraphrased.
Augustine, City of God 16.37, reads Jacob's deception as a mystery (not a lie). Confirm citation.
'Genesis never records her seeing him again': Rebecca's death isn't narrated; her nurse Deborah's death is (35:8). Confirm phrasing.
'Three times' Jacob lies: 27:19 (I am Esau thy firstborn), 27:20 (the Lord thy God sent it), 27:24 (I am). Confirm.
CCC 2482–2487 on lying and reparation. Confirm.
